originalTitle: The rise of south-east Asia’s girl bands: ‘The talent and popularity were always here’
summary: Girl bands from the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand are going global with their fusion of traditional and modern sounds
content: “We all know that music is a universal language,” says Maloi Ricalde from Filipina girl band BINI, which mixes tropical pop with traditional songs, English with Tagalog, and silver knee highs with pastel colours. “Incorporating Filipino language, Filipino culture, Filipino sound, into our music, it really gives identity and meaning to our music,” Ricalde tells the Guardian. Months after becoming the first south-east Asian girl band to perform at Coachella, and now with a tour of Japan under its belt, the group is enjoying a surge in popularity. “Our next goal,” says BINI member Jhoanna Robles, “Is that we want Filipino culture, Filipino music to be part of a conversation naturally on a global stage.” BINI is not the only girl group from south-east Asia to recently gain wider traction, with other girl bands such as Indonesia’s no na, Thailand’s 4EVE, and Malaysia’s DOLLA taking to stages around the world, instigating viral dance challenges and racking up millions of views online. Industry experts say musical talent has always existed in the region, but the infrastructure is now backing it up after the huge popularity of K-pop showed that investment could push Asian artists into the mainstream. The music industry in the west largely ignored Asian music before the 2012 hit Gangnam Style, which went viral in part thanks to its popularity in the Philippines and among its diaspora, says Piyapong Muenprasertdee, co-founder of music platform Fungjai. Many emerging artists and groups from the region are now gaining fans by blending modern and traditional elements, adds Piyapong. In Thailand indie acts as well as girl bands such as BNK48 are putting their own spin on local folk music Molam and Thai country music known as Luk Thung. In Vietnam and the Philippines, unique electronic dance music styles are becoming increasingly prominent in local club scenes. In Indonesia, girl band no na has mixed dangdut, a high-intensity genre with Indonesian, Malay, Arabic and Indian roots, with reggaeton and pop, including in their hit bilingual song Rollerblade, which has garnered 16m views. The group produces catchy, sometimes expletive-laden pop songs that feature traditional ceng-ceng cymbals, and gamelan, an ensemble from Java and Bali, which they perform in striking costumes and with occasional back-bending moves. “It’s been a consistent formula throughout our work process to find songs that have a global sound and add Indonesian elements as a cherry on top as our no na stamp,” the group tells the Guardian. “Because we’re a global girl group but still representing our country, we always try to find that balance without compromising too much of one or the other.” Thai girl group 4EVE reflects local elements like Bangkok’s bustling street culture in their music videos, while Malaysia’s DOLLA has released songs such as Raya Raya Raya celebrating the end of Ramadan, which they perform in modest, but hot-pink kaftans. One feature of Asian pop culture, says PR expert Bettina Miski, is the prominence of fandom and fanclubs, which have contributed to their popularity. “The relationship between the artists and the fans is a lot deeper,” says Miski, who runs a YouTube series called “THAI T”, which connects Asian artists with global audiences. “That devotion leads to spreading the word, a type of promotion that often goes beyond traditional marketing as it feels a lot more personal or intimate.” Girl bands in the region have special names for their fans, which provide support at concerts and online, including in posting dance challenges. BINI’s fans are called “Blooms”, for no na it’s “Orchids”, 4EVE’s “For Aye” (also meaning forever), and DOLLA’s “iDollas”. The row over the Grammys’ new category for Asian pop suggests inclusivity in the industry still has a way to go. The move was criticised for potentially ringfencing Asian pop artists from contending in the top categories. It also explicitly mentioned only K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop despite the region’s diversity. Still, says Piyapong, south-east Asia is well positioned to be “the next powerhouse” in the global music landscape. “We just recently entered an era where borders or language matter less,” says Miski, “The talent and popularity were always here, the system just had to catch up.”
chineseTitle: 东南亚女子乐队的崛起：“才华和人气一直都在这里”
chineseSummary: 来自菲律宾、印度尼西亚、马来西亚和泰国的女子乐队正在凭借传统与现代声音的融合走向全球
chineseContent: “我们都知道音乐是一种通用语言，”菲律宾女子乐队 BINI 的 Maloi Ricalde 说道，该乐队将热带流行音乐与传统歌曲、英语与他加禄语以及银色及膝高跟鞋与柔和的色彩融为一体。 “将菲律宾语言、菲律宾文化、菲律宾声音融入我们的音乐中，这确实为我们的音乐赋予了身份和意义，”里卡尔德告诉《卫报》。在成为第一个在科切拉音乐节演出的东南亚女子乐队几个月后，现在又开始了日本巡演，该乐队的受欢迎程度正在飙升。 “我们的下一个目标，”BINI 成员乔安娜·罗伯斯 (Jhoanna Robles) 说道，“我们希望菲律宾文化、菲律宾音乐自然地成为全球舞台上对话的一​​部分。” BINI 并不是唯一一个最近获得更广泛关注的东南亚女子组合，印度尼西亚的 no na、泰国的 4EVE 和马来西亚的 DOLLA 等其他女子组合也在世界各地登上舞台，发起了病毒式舞蹈挑战，并在网上获得了数百万的观看次数。行业专家表示，该地区一直存在音乐人才，但在韩国流行音乐的巨大流行表明投资可以将亚洲艺术家推向主流之后，基础设施正在为其提供支持。音乐平台 Fungjai 联合创始人 Piyapong Muenprasertdee 表示，在 2012 年热门歌曲《江南 Style》之前，西方音乐界基本上忽视了亚洲音乐，《江南 Style》的火爆部分归功于其在菲律宾及其海外侨民中的受欢迎程度。 Piyapong 补充道，该地区的许多新兴艺术家和团体现在通过融合现代和传统元素赢得了粉丝。在泰国，独立音乐人和 BNK48 等女子乐队正在将自己的风格融入当地民间音乐 Molam 和泰国乡村音乐 Luk Thung 中。在越南和菲律宾，独特的电子产品
